stops.title: Inventing Community Life in Vercelli
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Vercellae (Duomo di Sant’Eusebio) to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Peaceful sunlit northern Italian cathedral cloister where a smiling fourth-century bishop shares a simple wooden dinner table and ancient parchment Gospels with joyful parish priests.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Vercelli’s magnificent **Cathedral of St. Eusebius** still guards the astonishing **Codex Vercellensis**—a priceless 4th-century silver-ink Latin Gospel manuscript traditionally copied right by St. Eusebius’s own hand!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: That 1,660-year-old handwritten **Codex Vercellensis** inside Vercelli’s Cathedral Museum is the **oldest surviving manuscript of the Old Latin Gospels in the entire world**!
stops.saintQuote: Prayer and friendship in community give strength for every parish road.

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Arriving in northern Italy, Eusebius pioneered a brilliant innovation nobody in Western Europe had ever tried before: instead of leaving parish priests isolated and lonely, he invited all his diocesan priests to **live together like a joyful monastic family** right beside the cathedral—praying, studying Scripture, sharing simple meals, and heading out each morning to serve Vercelli’s poor! St. Ambrose marveled that Eusebius was the very first Western bishop to unite the deep prayer of a monk with the active service of a city pastor.

stops.title: Unbroken Courage in Eastern Exile & Joyful Return
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Scythopolis (Beit She’an) & Vercelli to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.eraLabel: 355 – August 1, 371 · Scythopolis, Egypt & Return to Vercelli
stops.imageCaption: Sun-baked ancient Roman marble theater colonnades glowing in warm amber twilight where an elderly exiled Western bishop writes encouraging letters of peace to his distant Italian flock.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Even though he suffered six harsh years of exile, St. Eusebius welcomed former opponents back with open arms at the Council of Alexandria—winning hearts across Europe until his peaceful passing at age eighty-eight!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Notice how Eusebius healed a bitterly divided Church: fierce as a lion against imperial bullying, yet tender as a lamb welcoming repentant bishops back home!
stops.saintQuote: Stand like iron for truth, and open your arms like water for reconciliation.

hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Unbroken Courage in Eastern Exile & Joyful Return
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: When Arian Emperor Constantius II tried to bully Western bishops at the Council of Milan (355) into condemning St. Athanasius and denying Christ’s full divinity, fearless Eusebius pulled out the **Nicene Creed** right in front of the furious emperor and refused to sign! Banished for six grueling years to **Scythopolis** in the Holy Land, Cappadocia, and Egypt’s burning Thebaid desert, Eusebius endured beatings and starvation with radiant dignity—returning home in 362 alongside St. Hilary of Poitiers to heal Italy with gentleness instead of revenge!

stops.title: Sixteen Hours a Day of Mercy at the Basilica of Ars
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Basilique d’Ars to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Luminous sunlit French Romanesque-Byzantine sanctuary filled with warm candlelight and hundreds of grateful pilgrims waiting peacefully beside a carved oak confessional.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Inside the glowing **Basilica of Ars**, visitors can see St. John Vianney’s remarkably preserved incorrupt body, his tiny iron-bed rectory, and the humble oak confessional where he healed tens of thousands of hearts.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Proclaimed the official **Universal Patron Saint of Parish Priests** by Pope Pius XI in 1929, St. John Vianney proved that pure love outshines every textbook on earth!
stops.saintQuote: Private prayer is like straw scattered here and there; if you set it on fire, it makes a lot of little flames. But gather these straws into a bundle and light them, and you get a mighty fire rising like a column into the sky—that is public prayer!

stops.title: The Miracle of the August Snowfall on Esquiline Hill
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Mons Esquilinus, Roma to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Magical sunlit summer Roman hilltop unexpectedly blanketed in pristine sparkling white snow outlining the crisp floorplan of a great basilica beneath blue August skies.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Every single year on **August 5**, during solemn Mass inside Santa Maria Maggiore, thousands of **fragrant white rose petals** cascade down from the gilded coffered ceiling just like snowflakes—recreating the Miracle of the Snow!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Even the gleaming golden ceiling overhead holds a stunning piece of world history: it was gilded with the **very first gold brought back from the Americas by Christopher Columbus**, gifted by King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella of Spain!
stops.saintQuote: Where heaven touches earth, even midsummer blooms with snow-white grace.

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: High above the lapis-lazuli altar of the Pauline Chapel shines Rome’s most beloved icon: **Salus Populi Romani** ("Protectress / Health of the Roman People")—carried through the streets by Pope St. Gregory the Great during the terrifying 590 AD plague and honored by popes and ordinary Romans for over fourteen centuries! Pope Francis loved this icon so deeply that he stopped here with a bouquet of flowers before and after **every single one of his 45+ international trips**—and chose Santa Maria Maggiore right beside *Salus Populi Romani* as his own final resting place!

stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Standing atop Mount Tabor’s breezy oak-and-almond summit, pilgrims take in one of the most sweeping panoramic views in the entire Holy Land—seeing Nazareth’s hills on one side and the Sea of Galilee’s valley on the other!

stops.eraLabel: 1924 – Present · Basilica of the Transfiguration, Mount Tabor
stops.imageCaption: Golden sunlit limestone twin-towered Syrian-Romanesque basilica glowing inside with shimmering gold mosaics and radiant alabaster windows.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Designed by master Holy Land architect Antonio Barluzzi in 1924 over ancient 4th-century ruins, the breathtaking **Basilica of the Transfiguration** features twin side chapels honoring Moses and Elijah AND translucent golden **alabaster windows** that literally flood the altar in warm glowing sunlight every August 6!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Wait until you hear this architectural marvel: Barluzzi engineered the eastern windows of Mount Tabor’s basilica so that right on **August 6 (Feast of the Transfiguration)**, morning sunrise rays align straight onto the golden Transfiguration mosaic!
stops.saintQuote: Rise, and do not be afraid.

stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Vicenza’s elegant Renaissance squares remember the nobleman who discovered that real wealth is measured by how freely it is shared.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: St. Cajetan is celebrated around the globe—especially across Argentina and Latin America as **San Cayetano**—as the beloved **Patron Saint of Bread, Work, and Job Seekers!**

stops.imageCaption: Bustling sunlit historic Neapolitan portico framed by ancient Roman temple columns where grateful artisans and mothers receive fair zero-interest emergency loans from a smiling saintly priest.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Every **August 7**, hundreds of thousands of workers and job-seekers line up for blocks in Buenos Aires, Naples, and worldwide carrying wheat stalks and loaves of bread to ask **St. Cajetan (San Cayetano)** for **"Peace, Bread, and Work!"**
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Think how cool St. Cajetan was: he helped invent the **Banco di Napoli** to fight loan sharks, championed **Naples’s famous Christmas Nativity scenes**, AND became the global champion of fair employment!

hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Inventing Naples’s Zero-Interest People’s Bank!
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Moving south to **Naples** in 1533, practical Father Cajetan saw greedy loan sharks crushing poor Neapolitan families with predatory interest rates! Instead of just scolding them, genius Cajetan teamed up with charitable citizens in 1539 to launch the **Monte di Pietà**—a non-profit, **interest-free community credit bank** where working families could borrow emergency cash honestly without losing their homes! That very bank grew into the historic **Banco di Napoli**—one of the oldest continuously operating banking legacies in the world! Passing away peacefully on August 7, 1547, he even popularized the beloved Neapolitan wooden **Christmas Nativity crèche** (*Presepe*)!

stops.title: The Famous Horse-Stable Schoolhouse of Penola
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Penola Stable Schoolhouse, Coonawarra to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Rustic weathered Australian timber horse stable bathed in warm golden Outback sunlight transformed into a cheerful wooden classroom filled with laughing rural bush children and a smiling brown-habited young teacher.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: In **Penola, South Australia**, visitors can step right inside the lovingly reconstructed **Penola Stable Schoolhouse** and interpretive center honoring the birth of the Brown Joeys!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Mary MacKillop was so fearless about protecting vulnerable children and speaking up against abuse of power that a misled Adelaide bishop actually **wrongfully excommunicated her** for five months in 1871! Never once growing bitter, she prayed peacefully—and the bishop himself wept, lifted the ban on his deathbed, and Pope Pius IX warmly blessed her work in Rome!
stops.saintQuote: We are but travelers here—do all you can with the means at your disposal, and calmly leave the rest to God.

hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Scan the center-left horizon of the painting.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: The Famous Horse-Stable Schoolhouse of Penola
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: In **Penola**, twenty-four-year-old Mary teamed up with brilliant naturalist-priest **Father Julian Tenison Woods**—and when they couldn’t afford a fancy building, Mary’s brother John simply cleaned out a dusty old **disused horse stable**! On **St. Joseph’s Day, March 19, 1866**, Mary put on a simple black dress, opened the stable doors to 33 delighted bush kids, and launched the **Sisters of St. Joseph of the Sacred Heart** (the beloved **"Brown Joeys"**)! Riding horses across scorching Outback tracks, Mary and her sisters opened over **117 schools, orphanages, and refuges** across Australia and New Zealand!

stops.eraLabel: 1883 – August 8, 1909 · Mary MacKillop Place, North Sydney
stops.imageCaption: Sunlit sandstone heritage chapel nestled beside blooming jacarandas near sparkling Sydney Harbour honoring Australia’s joyful pioneer saint.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Overlooking the harbor in North Sydney, **Mary MacKillop Place** preserves her serene memorial chapel tomb and interactive museum—sharing her immortal Australian golden rule with every generation: **"Never see a need without doing something about it!"**
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: St. Mary MacKillop is the ONLY saint in Church history to have been wrongfully excommunicated by her own bishop and later canonized—making her an enduring hero of integrity, patience, and courage!

stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across University of Göttingen & Freiburg to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Lamp-lit wooden German university library at midnight where a radiant young woman scholar reads an open leather autobiography straight through till golden sunrise.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Philosophers worldwide still study Edith Stein’s pioneering work on **empathy** and human personhood—making her one of the sharpest women thinkers of the 20th century!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Notice how Edith NEVER abandoned or rejected her Jewish heritage after her baptism—writing proudly to a friend: *"I feel more deeply Jewish now than ever, because Jesus Himself is my kinsman by blood!"*
stops.saintQuote: Do not accept anything as the truth if it lacks love; and do not accept anything as love which lacks truth.

hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Philosophy of Empathy at Göttingen & Bad Bergzabern
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Studying under legendary philosopher Edmund Husserl at **Göttingen** and Freiburg, Edith earned a glowing *summa cum laude* doctorate in 1916 with her groundbreaking thesis ***On the Problem of Empathy***—while serving courageously as a Red Cross nurse in a typhus field hospital during World War I! Then one summer night in 1921 at a friend’s farmhouse in Bad Bergzabern, Edith pulled a book at random off the shelf: **St. Teresa of Ávila’s *Autobiography***. Riveted, she read straight through the entire night until dawn—closed the cover—and whispered quietly: **"This is the Truth!"** Baptized on New Year’s Day 1922, she became a celebrated national speaker championing women’s education and dignity.

detectiveClues.headline: Philosophy of Empathy at Göttingen & Bad Bergzabern
detectiveClues.clueText: Studying under legendary philosopher Edmund Husserl at **Göttingen** and Freiburg, Edith earned a glowing *summa cum laude* doctorate in 1916 with her groundbreaking thesis ***On the Problem of Empathy***—while serving courageously as a Red Cross nurse in a typhus field hospital during World War I! Then one summer night in 1921 at a friend’s farmhouse in Bad Bergzabern, Edith pulled a book at random off the shelf: **St. Teresa of Ávila’s *Autobiography***. Riveted, she read straight through the entire night until dawn—closed the cover—and whispered quietly: **"This is the Truth!"** Baptized on New Year’s Day 1922, she became a celebrated national speaker championing women’s education and dignity.

stops.eraLabel: August 7 – 10, 258 · San Lorenzo in Panisperna, Rome
stops.imageCaption: Sunlit Roman imperial marble courtyard filled with smiling blind beggars, widows, orphans, and lame citizens as a radiant young deacon sweeps his arm proudly toward them before an astonished Roman Prefect.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: In Rome’s Monti neighborhood, the historic Church of **San Lorenzo in Panisperna** still honors the legendary spot where St. Lawrence faced martyrdom with fearless good humor!

Hippolytus wept, begged Pontian’s forgiveness, urged all his followers back in Rome to reunite immediately under one bishop, AND Pope Pontian famously made history by **resigning the papacy on September 28, 235** so Rome could elect a healthy new Pope right away!

detectiveClues.headline: Unlikely Best Friends in the Mines of Sardinia
detectiveClues.clueText: In 235 AD, harsh Emperor Maximinus Thrax launched a sudden crackdown on Roman Church leaders—arresting BOTH legitimate **Pope Pontian** AND rival **Antipope Hippolytus** and shipping both enemies together in chains to hard labor in the notorious, malaria-ridden **silver and lead mines of Sardinia**! Facing suffering and death side by side in the dark mine shafts, everything petty suddenly melted away! Hippolytus wept, begged Pontian’s forgiveness, urged all his followers back in Rome to reunite immediately under one bishop, AND Pope Pontian famously made history by **resigning the papacy on September 28, 235** so Rome could elect a healthy new Pope right away!

stops.imageCaption: Sun-drenched Mediterranean olive-dotted hill overlooking deep blue sea horizons where a calm silver-haired elderly Italian tailor rallies hundreds of ordinary craftsmen with serene dignity.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: The peaceful sanctuary of **Santa Maria dei Martiri** crowns the Hill of Minerva overlooking the Adriatic—reminding every visitor that heroism wears ordinary work clothes.

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: On August 14, 1480, over **800 surviving ordinary men and boys** of Otranto (aged fifteen and up) were marched up the sunlit **Hill of Minerva** overlooking the sea and offered a stark choice: renounce Christ and live freely, or die on the spot. Into the hushed silence stepped NOT a famous bishop or nobleman, but a humble elderly wool-shearer and tailor named **Antonio Pezzulla ("Primaldo")**! Looking calmly around at his trembling neighbors, Antonio spoke up clearly: *"My brothers, until today we fought to save our lives—now let us stand firm for Christ who gave His life for us!"* Instantly all 800 cheered in unison! Astonished by Antonio’s serene courage, even an Ottoman officer named **Bersabei** reportedly laid down his sword and confessed Christ on the spot!

globeHeaderSubtitle: Sacred Trails of St. Hyacinth of Poland (Rome, Kraków (Poland) & Kyiv (Ukraine))
completionSummary: You trekked thousands of miles across Central and Eastern Europe with joyful Dominican pioneer St. Hyacinth of Poland—"the Apostle of the North," who received his white habit directly from St. Dominic, rescued sacred treasures during the siege of Kyiv, AND is affectionately remembered as the Patron Saint of Pierogi!

stops.title: Meeting St. Dominic at Santa Sabina in Rome
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Santa Sabina, Aventine Hill, Rome to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Sunlit ancient Roman orange-grove cloister on Aventine Hill where smiling St. Dominic drapes a crisp white Dominican wool tunic over the shoulders of an eager young Polish scholar.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Step into the sunlit courtyard of **Santa Sabina** in Rome to see the ancient orange tree tradition says St. Dominic himself planted—the exact spot where St. Hyacinth launched his epic northern mission!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Wait until you hear why Polish grandmothers still exclaim **"Święty Jacku z pierogami!" ("St. Hyacinth and his pierogi!")** when surprised: legend says when hungry storms wiped out village harvests, compassionate St. Hyacinth prayed all night for the crops AND fed starving peasants warm steamed dumplings (*pierogi*)—making him Poland’s cheerful **Patron Saint of Pierogi!**
stops.saintQuote: Rejoice, my brothers—go north and carry the light of joy to every town!

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Born Jacek (Hyacinth) Odrowąż in Silesia around 1185 and educated in Kraków, Prague, and Bologna, the gifted young canon traveled to Rome in 1220 with his uncle Bishop Ivo of Kraków—where he witnessed **St. Dominic de Guzmán** perform a startling miracle raising a young nobleman back to life after a riding accident! Captivated instantly by Dominic’s joyful simplicity, Hyacinth knelt at **Santa Sabina** to receive the brand-new white-and-black Dominican habit directly from St. Dominic’s own hands—and set off straight north across the Alps to plant the Dominicans in Poland!

stops.title: The Unforgettable Rescue Across the Dnieper in Kyiv
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Kyiv, Dnieper Riverbank to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Dramatic smoky twilight along the icy sweeping Dnieper River as a fearless white-robed friar strides calmly across the water clutching a golden ciborium in one hand and a glowing stone statue of Mary in the other.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Because he rescued the heavy statue and carried it safely across the Dnieper River, St. Hyacinth is ALSO cheerfully invoked as the **Patron Saint of Weightlifters**—how awesome is that?!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Patron Saint of **Pierogi AND Weightlifters** AND Apostle of Poland, Ukraine, and the Baltics—St. Hyacinth might genuinely have the most fun, joyful résumé in the entire Calendar of Saints!
stops.saintQuote: Nothing carried out of love ever feels too heavy.

hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: The Unforgettable Rescue Across the Dnieper in Kyiv
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Walking all the way east to **Kyiv** to build warm friendship with Eastern Christians, Hyacinth was celebrating Mass in December 1240 when terrifying Mongol invaders burst through Kyiv’s gates! Racing to the altar to rescue the **Blessed Sacrament** in a golden ciborium, Hyacinth turned to flee—when legend says the heavy stone **statue of the Virgin Mary** called out tenderly: *"Hyacinth, my son—would you carry away my Son and leave His Mother behind?"* Smiling through tears, Hyacinth reached out and found the heavy alabaster statue miraculously **light as a feather**—carrying BOTH safely across the broad Dnieper River!

stops.imageCaption: Soaring pale Norman limestone Gothic twin spires rising near breezy Channel cliffs illuminated in warm golden afternoon light.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Just minutes from Normandy’s coast, the radiant **Basilica of Our Lady of La Délivrande** cherishes St. John Eudes’s favorite pilgrimage shrine—reminding us that the twin Hearts of Jesus and Mary beat with unstoppable warmth!

stops.title: Turning "Valley of Bitterness" into Clairvaux ("Valley of Light")
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Clara Vallis (Clairvaux) to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Peaceful sunlit forested French river valley cleared into blooming orchards, humming watermills, and crisp whitewashed stone abbey arches bathed in golden morning glow.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Bernard’s luminous Marian hymn *"Look to the Star, Call on Mary"*—and his heartfelt advice to a busy Pope (*"Be a reservoir that fills up first before overflowing to others, never an empty dry canal!"*)—still inspire leaders and contemplatives 900 years later!

stops.saintQuote: In dangers, in doubts, in difficulties—think of Mary, call upon Mary! Look to the Star!

stops.title: Smiling Patriarch of Venice on the Grand Canal
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Patriarcato di Venezia (San Marco) to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Glowing golden Byzantine domes of St. Mark’s Basilica reflected across shimmering Venetian canals as a kindly smiling white-haired Cardinal chats warmly with ordinary gondoliers on a stone bridge.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Venice still treasures its beloved Patriarch Beppo—honored across the lagoon and inside St. Mark’s Basilica where he restored joyful choral music.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Even after becoming Pope in Rome, Pius X missed his beloved Venice and family so dearly that his two humble unmarried sisters moved into a modest attic apartment at the Vatican to mend his socks and cook him simple Veneto polenta!

hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Scan the center-left horizon of the painting.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Smiling Patriarch of Venice on the Grand Canal
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Named Cardinal-Patriarch of **Venice** in 1893, warmhearted Giuseppe Sarto stunned stiff aristocrats by ditching pomp, riding public canal boats chatting with fishermen in lively Venetian dialect, handing out candies to barefoot lagoon kids, and pawning his own episcopal ring whenever a starving family needed rent! stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Basilica di San Pietro, Vatican to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.eraLabel: 1903 – August 20, 1914 · St. Peter’s Basilica, Vatican City
stops.imageCaption: Warm golden sunbeams streaming across St. Peter’s Basilica as a gentle smiling white-robed pope bends down lovingly to greet bright-eyed young seven-year-old children approaching the altar.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Resting inside a luminous bronze-and-crystal shrine right on the main floor of **St. Peter’s Basilica**, **Pope St. Pius X** broke his heart pleading vainly for European kings to stop World War I—passing away peacefully on August 20, 1914 just weeks after war erupted.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Every smiling seven-year-old walking down a church aisle on First Holy Communion morning—and every adult welcomed joyfully to frequent Communion—is celebrating the gift of **Pope St. Pius X!**
stops.saintQuote: Holy Communion is the shortest and safest way to heaven.

hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: "Pope of the Eucharist" & Children’s First Communion in Rome
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Before Pope St. Pius X, strict old customs forced children to wait until ages **12 to 14** for First Holy Communion—and scared ordinary adults into receiving Communion barely once or twice a year! Smiling warmly with common-sense love, Pope Pius X shattered that cold wall forever: declaring that the Eucharist is **"NOT a prize for the perfect, but daily medicine and bread for the hungry!"**, he invited everyone to **frequent and daily Communion** AND lowered the age of **First Holy Communion down to age seven**—saying gently: *"Let the little children come to Me!"*

stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Right in central Lima, pilgrims flock to the **Sanctuary of St. Rose of Lima**—where her tiny adobe garden hermitage AND the famous **Wishing Well (Pozo de los Deseos)** overflow with thousands of handwritten prayer letters every August!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: St. Rose of Lima was close friends and neighbors with BOTH **St. Martin de Porres** AND **St. John Macias**—imagine THREE canonized saints walking the exact same sunny Lima blocks and swapping herbs for the poor!

detectiveClues.clueText: Born **Isabel Flores de Oliva** in **Lima, Peru** in 1586, she was nicknamed **"Rose"** as a baby after a loving Indigenous servant marveled that the sleeping infant’s face looked like a blooming rose! When her father’s silver-mining business failed, industrious young Rose stepped right up—staying awake late sewing exquisite lace and growing vibrant garden flowers to sell at Lima’s market to support her entire family AND buy medicine for the poor! stops.title: Turning Her Parents’ Home into a Free Clinic for All
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Lima Colonial Quarter to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Warm candlelit colonial Peruvian plaster room lined with woven blankets and healing herbal bowls where a smiling young woman in a white Dominican veil tenderly nurses elderly Indigenous and African neighbors.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Because she grew flowers for the poor and healed bodies with tenderness, St. Rose is honored as the official **Patron Saint of the Americas, the Philippines, Gardeners, and Florists**!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Legend laughs warmly that even Lima’s buzzing evening **mosquitoes** respected St. Rose—staying politely silent in her garden hermitage whenever she invited them to join her in singing praises to God!
stops.saintQuote: When we serve the poor and the sick, we serve Jesus!

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: Find the luminous focal point of Lima Colonial Quarter in the scene.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Scan the center-left horizon of the painting.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Turning Her Parents’ Home into a Free Clinic for All
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Rose didn’t lock herself away in her garden—she literally turned a big room inside her parents’ own house into a **free clinic and soup kitchen** specifically welcoming abandoned Indigenous Peruvians, enslaved African laborers, and homeless elders whom fancy colonial hospitals ignored! When her startled mother protested that bringing poor strangers indoors was messy, Rose smiled gently and answered: **"When we serve the poor and the sick, we serve Jesus Himself!"**

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Identified across Christian tradition with **Nathanael of Cana** (*Bar-Tolmai* means "Son of Tolmai"!), **St. Bartholomew** won Jesus’s heart in literally five seconds flat with his hilarious, refreshingly blunt honesty! When his excited friend Philip ran up saying, *"We’ve found the Messiah—Jesus of Nazareth!"*, skeptical Nathanael raised an eyebrow and blurted straight out: **"Can anything good come out of Nazareth?!"** Philip grinned: *"Come and see!"* And the moment Nathanael walked up, Jesus smiled wide and praised him: **"Here is a true Israelite—there is ZERO phoniness in him!"** When Jesus added *"Before Philip called you, I saw you under the fig tree,"* stunned Nathanael dropped his skepticism on the spot!

stops.imageCaption: Sun-dappled emerald medieval oak grove outside Paris where a smiling barefoot French king in a plain blue wool cloak sits casually on a mossy lawn listening intently to ordinary farmers and widows.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Every visitor to Paris’s Bois de Vincennes—and every resident of **St. Louis, Missouri** (proudly named after him!)—remembers the king who traded royal arrogance for radical fairness.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: King Louis IX was SO widely trusted as the most honest referee in Europe that even rival English King Henry III and his rebellious English barons voluntarily hired French King Louis as their neutral peace arbitrator!

stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Standing inside the Upper Chapel of **Sainte-Chapelle** in Paris feels like stepping inside a giant shimmering sapphire jewel—AND King Louis ALSO founded Paris’s **Quinze-Vingts** (Europe’s oldest still-operating eye hospital for 300 blind citizens!) and supported the **Sorbonne University**!

stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Every morning at 6:00 AM inside **Jasna Góra**, brass fanfare trumpets sound as a gleaming silver screen slowly rises to unveil the scarred, radiant face of **Our Lady of Częstochowa** before thousands of hushed pilgrims!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: In 1655 during "The Deluge," when invading Swedish armies had conquered virtually all of Poland, tiny hilltop Jasna Góra—defended by just 70 monks and 160 volunteers!—miraculously held out for 40 days, inspiring Poland’s revival and leading King John II Casimir to crown Mary **"Queen of Poland"** in 1656!
stops.saintQuote: Look upon her scarred cheek and know she understands every human wound.

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Rescuing the treasured icon from war-torn **Belz Castle** (in today’s western Ukraine) in 1382, Prince Władysław of Opole loaded it onto a wagon heading west—until legend tells the horses mysteriously stopped dead on a sunlit limestone hill above **Częstochowa** and refused to budge! Founding a Pauline monastery on that hill—named **Jasna Góra ("Bright Mountain")**—the monks treasured the icon right through a harrowing 1430 raid when bandits slashed Mary’s right cheek TWICE with a saber! Restorers tried painting over the two scars, yet the dark slashes kept reappearing—becoming the icon’s unforgettable badge of solidarity with every wounded human heart!

stops.title: Walking 200 Miles & the 9:00 PM Jasna Góra Appeal
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Apel Jasnogórski, Częstochowa to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Glowing lantern-lit August pilgrimage square packed with hundreds of thousands of smiling backpack-wearing young pilgrims singing joyfully beneath starry Polish twilight skies.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Inside Jasna Góra’s Chapel of the Miraculous Image hangs Pope St. John Paul II’s pierced blood-stained white sash from the 1981 assassination attempt—placed right beside the Black Madonna in eternal gratitude!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: On **August 26** every year, Poland celebrates **Our Lady of Częstochowa** as a radiant day of national thanksgiving—and **St. Pope John Paul II** placed a tiny replica of her scarred face in his own private study!

stops.title: Peacemaker Wife & Mother in Thagaste, North Africa
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Thagaste, Numidia to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Warm sunlit North African stone courtyard framed by ancient olive trees where a calm, patient Berber Christian mother listens warmly while her restless brilliant teenage son argues passionately over scrolls.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Across the globe, parents weeping over prodigal children find instant courage in St. Monica—the woman who proved gentle, stubborn love outlasts every storm.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: When distraught Monica begged an exhausted elderly bishop in Carthage to debate her stubborn teenage son Augustine, the wise bishop smiled gently and spoke history’s most comforting line for parents: **"Go in peace—it is impossible that the son of so many tears should perish!"**
stops.saintQuote: It is impossible that the child of so many tears should be lost!

hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Peacemaker Wife & Mother in Thagaste, North Africa
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Born into a Berber Christian family in **Thagaste** (modern Souk Ahras, Algeria) around 332, **Monica** wasn’t born a plaster statue—she actually struggled as a young girl with sneaking sweet wine from her parents’ cellar until a blunt servant girl teased her, curing her forever! Married off to **Patricius**—a quick-tempered, unfaithful pagan husband with a fierce live-in mother-in-law!—wise Monica discovered a genius secret: **never shout back while someone is furious; wait calmly until the storm passes, then speak with warmth and respect!** By sheer radiant patience, she won BOTH her prickly mother-in-law AND her husband Patricius to baptism before he died!

stops.title: Chasing a Runaway Son Across the Sea to Milan
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Mediolanum (Baptistery of San Giovanni, Milan) to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Candlelit octagonal fourth-century marble baptistery in Milan where a radiant weeping mother watches in overflowing joy as Bishop St. Ambrose baptizes her smiling grown son.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Beneath the sweeping floor of Milan’s giant Duomo, visitors can still step right down to the excavated 4th-century octagonal marble **Baptistery of San Giovanni** where St. Monica saw her seventeen-year prayer answered!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Think about how funny and real St. Augustine’s *Confessions* is: Augustine admits God answered Monica’s TRUE prayer—NOT her panicky prayer begging "Don’t let him sail to Italy!", because sailing to Italy was the exact road that led Augustine straight to St. Ambrose!
stops.saintQuote: Nothing is far from God!

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: Find the luminous focal point of Mediolanum (Baptistery of San Giovanni, Milan) in the scene.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Scan the center-left horizon of the painting.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Chasing a Runaway Son Across the Sea to Milan
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: When twenty-nine-year-old Augustine literally tricked his mother one night at Carthage’s harbor—telling her to wait inside a seaside chapel while he secretly hopped aboard a ship to Italy without her!—unstoppable Monica simply booked passage on the **very next boat** and tracked him straight north to **Milan**! There she became close friends with Milan’s magnetic Bishop **St. Ambrose**—who even listened respectfully to Monica’s sharp philosophical questions during family discussions at Cassiciacum! On **Easter Vigil, April 24, 387**, Monica wept happy tears watching St. Ambrose baptize her son Augustine AND her grandson Adeodatus!

stops.title: The Golden Window at Ostia & Shrine in Rome
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Ostia Tiberina & Sant’Agostino, Rome to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.eraLabel: Autumn 387 · Ostia Antica & Basilica of Sant’Agostino, Rome
stops.imageCaption: Peaceful Roman harbor garden window bathed in warm golden Mediterranean twilight as a joyful silver-haired mother and her transformed son lean together gazing out toward eternal starry skies.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Just steps from Rome’s Piazza Navona inside the luminous **Basilica of Sant’Agostino**, pilgrims pray beside St. Monica’s green-marble tomb—and her feast day (**August 27**) stands lovingly right the day BEFORE her son **St. Augustine’s feast day (August 28)!**
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Oh—and yes, sunny **Santa Monica, California** got its gorgeous seaside name when Spanish explorers arrived right around St. Monica’s spring feast day and saw sparkling crystal springs reminding them of St. Monica’s joyful tears!
stops.saintQuote: Lay this body anywhere; only this I ask of you—that you remember me at the altar of the Lord, wherever you are!

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: Find the luminous focal point of Ostia Tiberina & Sant’Agostino, Rome in the scene.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Scan the center-left horizon of the painting.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: The Golden Window at Ostia & Shrine in Rome
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Waiting at Rome’s sunny port of **Ostia** to sail back home to North Africa together, mother and son leaned side by side out of a quiet garden window one unforgettable golden afternoon—talking so deeply about the joy of heaven that time seemed to vanish! Turning to Augustine with serene peace, fifty-five-year-old Monica smiled: *"Son, my one remaining reason to linger in this life was to see you a Christian before I died—and God has given me even more than I ever asked!"* Falling ill five days later, when Augustine worried about burying her far from home in Africa, Monica grinned one last time: **"Bury this body anywhere at all—only remember me at the altar of the Lord wherever you may be!"**

stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across ancient Thagaste to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Hillside of Souk Ahras, Algeria (ancient Thagaste), where the living Olive Tree of St. Augustine still stands.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Today, ancient Thagaste is the Algerian mountain town of Souk Ahras. On a quiet hill overlooking the town, pilgrims still visit the living "Olive Tree of St. Augustine" (El-Zitouna), where tradition holds he sat in contemplation.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: In Book II of his Confessions, Augustine famously confessed to stealing pears from a neighbor’s tree at age 16—not because he was hungry, since he threw the fruit to pigs, but purely for the thrill of doing wrong with his friends.
stops.saintQuote: “You have made us for Yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in You.”
stops.detectiveCaseTitle: Case #1 · The Mountain Town of the Thousand-Year Olive Tree

detectiveClues.headline: An Inland Mountain Town in Northeastern Algeria
detectiveClues.clueText: In Roman times this town was called Thagaste. Today it is an inland mountain city in northeastern Algeria near the Tunisian border, where locals still protect a living 1,000-year-old olive tree ("Zitouna Saint Augustin") on a hillside overlooking the town.

detectiveClues.headline: The Confessed Midnight Pear Heist
detectiveClues.clueText: At age 16 in this town, young Augustine and his friends shook down a huge load of pears from a neighbor’s orchard at night—not to eat them (they threw them to hogs!), but strictly for the thrill of doing what was forbidden.

detectiveClues.headline: Born Here in 354 AD to St. Monica & Patricius
detectiveClues.clueText: Many people don’t realize St. Augustine was North African! He was born in this Algerian hillside town in 354 AD, and returned here in 388 AD after his baptism to establish his very first monastery.

stops.title: The Spark of Wisdom by the Sea
stops.subtitle: Search the sunset harbor of Carthage to uncover 3 hidden clues
stops.imageCaption: Roman harbor columns of ancient Carthage on the Mediterranean coast of modern Tunis, Tunisia.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Today, ancient Carthage is a scenic coastal suburb of Tunis, the capital of Tunisia. You can walk beside the Roman Antonine Baths, the seaside columns, and the amphitheater where early Christian martyrs gave their lives.

stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: In modern-day Milan, Italy, you can go down the stairs beneath the front square of the famous Milan Cathedral (Duomo di Milano) and stand beside the actual 8-sided brick pool where St. Ambrose baptized St. Augustine at Easter in 387 AD!

detectiveClues.headline: Four Meters Underneath the Duomo Square in Northern Italy
detectiveClues.clueText: Known in Roman times as Mediolanum, this major northern Italian city is famous today for fashion and its white-marble Gothic Duomo. Right beneath the front steps of the Duomo lies the preserved 8-sided brick pool where Augustine was baptized!

detectiveClues.headline: The Bishop Who Read Without Moving His Lips!
detectiveClues.clueText: In the ancient world, manuscripts had no spaces between words, so everyone read out loud. When Augustine visited Bishop St. Ambrose here, he was astonished to watch Ambrose reading a book in complete silence without moving his tongue!

detectiveClues.headline: “Tolle, Lege!” (“Take Up and Read!”) Under the Fig Tree
detectiveClues.clueText: Weeping in a garden here in August 386 AD, Augustine heard a child chanting "Tolle, lege!" ("Take up and read!"). Opening Romans 13:13, his heart was transformed, and St. Ambrose baptized him here at Easter Vigil 387 AD.

stops.saintQuote: “In my Father’s house there are many resting places… our peace is our rest, and our rest is in the fullness of love.”

stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Fun fact: when Aidan died at Bamburgh on August 31, 651, a young teenage shepherd boy watching sheep far up in the misty hills saw radiant angels carrying a shining soul to heaven—that very boy was **St. Cuthbert**, who walked down the next morning to become a monk!
stops.saintQuote: Is the son of a mare dearer to you than a child of God?

hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Giving Away the King’s Royal Horse at Bamburgh
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Wait until you hear the funniest story St. Bede tells about St. Aidan! Worried that aging Aidan walked too many miles barefoot across rocky rivers, generous King Oswine gifted Aidan a **magnificent, royally saddled thoroughbred horse**! Literally the very first afternoon Aidan rode it out from **Bamburgh**, a poor shivering beggar asked for alms—so Aidan hopped straight off and **handed the beggar the King’s prized royal horse AND its fancy gilded saddle!** When startled King Oswine teased him over dinner (*"Wait, didn’t I have cheaper horses for beggars?!"*), twinkling-eyed Aidan grinned straight back: **"Your Majesty—is the son of a mare dearer to you than a child of God?"** The King knelt laughing in admiration and promised never to complain about Aidan’s generosity again! Dying peacefully leaning against the wooden beam of **Bamburgh’s church** on August 31, 651, Aidan left northern England glowing forever with joy.
